summary: Lanthanum carbonate is a non-aluminum, non-calcium phosphate binder used to reduce serum phosphate in patients with end-stage renal disease. It is taken as chewable tablets with or immediately after meals, where lanthanum binds dietary phosphate into insoluble complexes eliminated in the feces, with very low systemic absorption. The most common adverse effects are gastrointestinal (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain) and generally lessen over time. Tablets must be chewed or crushed completely to avoid serious gastrointestinal complications, and the drug is radio-opaque, which can mimic an imaging agent on abdominal X-rays. Because it binds many co-administered oral drugs, dosing of interacting medications must be separated.

moa: Lanthanum carbonate is a phosphate binder that reduces absorption of dietary phosphate by forming insoluble lanthanum phosphate complexes that pass through the gastrointestinal tract unabsorbed. Lanthanum binds phosphate across the physiologically relevant pH range of 3 to 7 (approximately 97% of available phosphate at pH 3-5 and 67% at pH 7 in simulated gastric fluid). Because it must contact dietary phosphate in the gut, it is given with or immediately after meals. Both serum phosphate and the calcium-phosphate product fall as a consequence of reduced dietary phosphate absorption. Systemic absorption of lanthanum is very low (bioavailability <0.002%).

Bowel obstruction, including ileus and fecal impaction

preg: Available human case-report data are insufficient to identify a drug-associated risk of major birth defects or miscarriage. In animal studies, doses about 5 times the maximum recommended human dose in rabbits caused maternal toxicity, increased post-implantation loss, reduced fetal weights, and delayed ossification, and lanthanum deposits into developing bone. The label advises using a non-lanthanum containing phosphate binder in a pregnant woman.
lact: There are no data on the presence of lanthanum in human milk, its effects on the breastfed infant, or on milk production. Because lanthanum deposits into developing bone in juvenile animals, the label advises using a non-lanthanum containing phosphate binder in a lactating woman.
renal: Lanthanum carbonate is indicated specifically to treat hyperphosphatemia in patients with end-stage renal disease, so renal impairment is its intended population; no separate renal dose adjustment is provided. In dialysis patients, plasma lanthanum was cleared with an elimination half-life of about 53 hours after discontinuation.
hepatic: The label does not provide a specific dose adjustment for hepatic impairment. Lanthanum is not metabolized and is eliminated predominantly via biliary excretion of the small absorbed fraction; in animal studies, hepatic lanthanum levels rose with renal impairment due to greater intestinal absorption.

major: Oral quinolone antibiotics (e.g., ciprofloxacin) - absorption markedly reduced (ciprofloxacin AUC reduced ~54%); give quinolone at least 1 hour before or 4 hours after lanthanum carbonate
Levothyroxine / thyroid hormone replacement - bioavailability reduced ~40%; separate by at least 2 hours before or after lanthanum carbonate and monitor TSH
moderate: Compounds whose absorption is reduced by cationic antacids (aluminum-, magnesium-, calcium-based) - e.g., ampicillin, tetracyclines, ACE inhibitors, statins, anti-malarials; do not give within 2 hours of lanthanum carbonate
Other oral medications with a clinically significant absorption-dependent effect - consider separating dosing times and monitoring response/levels
minor: Drugs with a narrow therapeutic range taken orally - consider monitoring clinical response or blood levels
interactions.food: Take with or immediately after meals to bind dietary phosphate; the timing of food relative to dosing has a negligible effect on systemic lanthanum exposure.
interactions.alcohol: No specific alcohol interaction is described in the labeling.
interactions.diagnostics: Lanthanum carbonate is radio-opaque and may give the appearance of an imaging agent on abdominal X-rays; product residue has been reported during endoscopic imaging.

rare: Tooth injury while chewing the tablet

monitoring: Serum phosphate during dose titration (every 2-3 weeks) and regularly thereafter
Gastrointestinal symptoms suggestive of obstruction, ileus, or perforation
TSH if co-administered with thyroid hormone replacement

pearls: Non-aluminum, non-calcium phosphate binder - useful when avoiding calcium load or aluminum toxicity in ESRD
Must be chewed or crushed completely and taken with/immediately after meals to work; intact tablets risk serious GI complications
Radio-opaque - can mimic an imaging agent on abdominal X-ray and may leave residue at endoscopy
Binds co-administered oral drugs: separate quinolones (1 h before / 4 h after) and levothyroxine (2 h either side), and monitor TSH
Lanthanum deposits in developing bone - avoid in pregnancy, lactation, and pediatric patients; use a non-lanthanum binder instead
missed: If you miss a dose, take it with your next meal; do not take a dose between meals and do not double up. Because the medicine works only on the phosphate in food, a dose taken without a meal has little benefit.
overdose: Overdose symptoms are adverse reactions such as headache, nausea, and vomiting; gastrointestinal symptoms were reported at daily doses up to 6,000 mg taken with food. Given the drug's topical action in the gut and predominantly fecal excretion, management is supportive.
